item.title: SEFCOM Research Internship
item.description:
This summer I attended a high school research internship at the SEFCOM lab, with Zion Basque, also known as mahaloz, as my mentor.

My work focused on improving the readability of the angr decompiler’s output through simplification passes. Within this post, I’ll walk through the formatting changes and control flow simplification I implemented, then look at their impact on the coreutils test suite.

Background

As a bit of background, decompilation1 is the process of lifting and simplifying low level code into higher level constructs. This allows a human to more efficiently analyze such abstractions which serves to aid in the process of static binary analysis and source code recovery.

item.title: Pwnable.tw: Unexploitable
item.description:
unexploitable [500 pts]

The original challenge is on pwnable.kr and it is solvable.

This time we fix the vulnerability and now we promise that the service is unexploitable.

nc chall.pwnable.tw 10403

unexploitable libc.so

Initial Analysis

By running checksec, we can view the protections and memory corruption mitigations enabled on this binary.

Arch: amd64-64-little
RELRO: Partial RELRO
Stack: No canary found
NX: NX enabled
PIE: No PIE (0x400000)

NX is enabled, so the stack is non-executable. There is no stack canary or PIE, and RELRO is only partial.

item.title: Sigreturn Oriented Programming
item.description:
Sigreturn oriented programming takes advantage of the signal handling mechanism on Unix based systems to gain control over a process’s execution context.

Within this post, I’ll cover how the technique works and how we can use it to construct a weird machine. First, we need to understand how signals are delivered, how the execution context is saved, and how it is restored when a handler returns.

Signal Handling

So what are signals, how do they work and what purpose do they serve?

Your choice :

The menu gives us a fair amount of control over the process heap. Let’s open the binary and look at its internals. If you are using Binary Ninja, a bndb is linked at the start of the post.

item.title: Glibc PTMalloc Internals
item.description:
The GNU C Library is complex, and its default memory allocator, PTMalloc, is no exception. Within this post, I’ll document the allocator’s internals and how they have evolved across versions of Glibc.

These notes grew out of years of being bombarded with heapnote challenges. I’m writing them partly for my own sake: keeping track of the differences between versions has become difficult without a reference.

We’ll start with the heap and chunk layout, then work through the bins, arenas, and allocation and deallocation algorithms. The algorithm walkthroughs focus on Glibc 2.31; keep the version in mind when comparing them with other releases.
